hints: Focus on what concentrated H2SO4 does to an alcohol, think elimination of water to form a C=C double bond.
Remember X starts as one pure optical isomer, so ask yourself what the alkene product must look like to avoid E/Z, cis/trans or enantiomer pairs.
Look for the alcohol that can only lose water in one way, even if by rearrangement, to give a single achiral alkene with no positional isomers.
walkthrough:
**Identify the reaction as dehydration**

Great start, let's see what is happening. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with heat dehydrates an alcohol to an alkene.

$$\text{R-OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4, \text{heat}} \text{alkene} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Understand the two conditions for only one product**

This is the key idea. To get only one organic product, there must be no positional isomerism and no stereoisomerism.

That means only one different type of H can be removed to form the C=C, and the alkene formed must be achiral with no cis-trans or E/Z options in the ring.

**Use the optical isomer clue**

You are told X is a single, pure, optical isomer. So X itself must be chiral and capable of showing enantiomerism.

But its dehydration product must NOT be chiral and must NOT show cis-trans isomerism, otherwise you would get two products from that one starting enantiomer.

**Test option D, the primary alcohol with rearrangement**

Option D is $(2\text{-methylcyclohexyl)methanol}$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})$. It is chiral at C1 and C2 of the ring, so it can exist as a pure optical isomer.

Loss of water gives a primary $\text{CH}_2^+$ carbocation, then a hydride shift from the ring gives a more stable tertiary carbocation at C2, and loss of $\text{H}^+$ gives only $1,2\text{-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene}$. This alkene has both methyl groups on the C=C, it is achiral and has no positional or stereoisomers in a six-membered ring. So only one product, perfect.

options.A: 3,4-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol is chiral, but dehydration removes H from C2 or C6 to give 3,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene and 4,5-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene type positions. More importantly, the product still has two saturated chiral centres at C3 and C4, so cis and trans forms and enantiomers are possible. More than one organic product forms.
options.B: 2,3-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol is chiral, but OH at C1 can lose H from C2 or C6 to give different positional alkenes, 2,3-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene versus 3,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene. The products retain chiral centres, so diastereomers and enantiomers are also possible. This gives a mixture, not one product.
options.C: 1,2-dimethylcyclohexan-1-ol is a tertiary alcohol and is chiral, but dehydration can remove H from C2 to give 1,2-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene or remove H from C6 to give 6-methyl-1-methylcyclohex-1-ene, where the second methyl is allylic not vinylic. These are two different positional alkenes, so more than one product forms.
options.D: D is (2-methylcyclohexyl)methanol, a chiral primary alcohol, so a pure optical isomer is possible. Dehydration via carbocation rearrangement leads to a single stable tertiary carbocation and then to only 1,2-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene. This alkene is achiral, the double bond is fixed cis in the ring, and there is no other position for the double bond of equal stability. Only one organic product is formed.
